reading.body:
Defense AI procurement is documented in free federal databases, SAM.gov, USAspending, and FPDS, with the Defense Innovation Unit as the commercial entry point and subscription analysts layered on top.

The free sources are the primary record. SAM.gov lists solicitations and awards, USAspending carries every federal award, and FPDS records contract actions and vendor performance at the transaction level. DIU is where commercial AI enters DoD programs, with public project listings. Govini builds decision science on that record, and Silicon Valley Defense Group maps the commercial entrants.

The programs of record are decision support, autonomy, and ISR processing, the AI applications the sector tracks. Tracking them through procurement data shows actual spending and vendor capability, not just announcements. What the data does not show is compute demand, building capacity, or power requirements, none of those appear in these sources. Government AI labs are catalogued separately, not here.

summary: Decision support, autonomy, and ISR processing are the programs of record; DIU is the commercial on-ramp. Who tracks the sector: free government procurement databases are the primary record, with dedicated defense-intelligence firms layered on top - this page starts with the sources anyone can verify.

analysis.body:
The material available for defense does not include a measured adoption rate. No Census Bureau figure appears in this JSON, and no source here reports a percentage of defense organizations using AI, so the honest starting point is that adoption in this sector is documented through procurement records and program descriptions rather than through survey statistics. What the sources do show is where the money and the paperwork live.

The federal procurement system is the primary evidence base. Per SAM.gov, the government's own system of record, AI-related Department of Defense solicitations, awards, and vendor registrations are free and searchable there, and SAM.gov has absorbed functions that used to sit elsewhere: the FPDS.gov "ezSearch" feature has been retired and users should conduct all contract awards data searches in SAM.gov, with the FPDS.gov ATOM Feed to be retired later in FY 2026. Per FPDS, the Federal Procurement Data System records DoD contract actions and vendor performance history at the transaction level, and the General Services Administration has retired the Electronic Subcontracting Reporting System, with subcontracting reporting capabilities now available in SAM.gov. Per USAspending, every federal award is downloadable, and contract spending on AI-related solutions traces there, built on the Federal Procurement Data System feed. For a reader trying to size this market, these three systems are the ground truth, and they are free.

The commercial on-ramp is named explicitly. Per DIU, the Defense Innovation Unit is where commercial AI enters DoD programs, with public project listings, and its stated mission is to convert entrepreneurial products into tangible combat power. Per Silicon Valley Defense Group, the nonprofit monitors the intersection of commercial tech, private capital, and national security and publicly maps the companies driving AI adoption in the DoD space. Per Govini, the defense-intelligence platform used inside the Department tracks procurement trends, supply-chain risk, and vendor capability in AI and autonomy and publishes public scorecards on critical-technology spending; its platform layer transforms activated data into adaptive workflows, mobilized agents, and AI-driven orchestration that proactively forecasts issues, prioritizes recommendations, and aligns resources. This site's own coverage frames the sector around decision support, autonomy, and ISR processing as programs of record, with DIU as the commercial on-ramp.

On the analysis side, Janes describes open source defence and security intelligence built on validated data, with experts acting as human sensors collecting data no web crawler could ever access, every data point verified against vetted sources, and final content peer reviewed to meet a decision-grade standard; it also describes shareable unclassified intelligence across domains and partners enabling interoperability and rapid alignment by design. Janes and Forecast International are named here as long-running defense analysis providers maintaining databases of contractors, programs, and procurement forecasts, and both are subscription sources. Government AI labs are catalogued separately on this site, which lists two individually verified organisations, Technology Innovation Institute in Abu Dhabi and Shanghai AI Laboratory in China, both state-funded and able to command infrastructure commitments, including compute and facilities, that market-driven labs must negotiate for commercially.

The regulatory posture visible in this material is procurement law rather than AI-specific rulemaking. Per SAM.gov, the system contains Controlled Unclassified Information and all individuals viewing, reproducing or disposing of it are required to protect it in accordance with 32 CFR Part 2002 and GSA Order CIO 2103.2 CUI Policy, and the system is subject to monitoring with unauthorized activities subject to disciplinary action including criminal prosecution. The same page notes Executive Order 13658, which generally applies to contracts subject to the Service Contract Act or the Davis-Bacon Act awarded between January 1, 2015, and January 29, 2022, and not renewed or extended on or after January 30, 2022, setting a minimum wage of $13.65 per hour for workers performing on covered contracts. These are the compliance contours a vendor actually encounters.

What a reader deciding whether to deploy should take from this is narrower than a market forecast. The sources here do not report ROI evidence for defense AI, and none of them quantify cost savings or performance gains, so any such claim would be unsupported by this material. What they do support is a path: watch SAM.gov for solicitations and awards, trace spending through USAspending and FPDS, treat DIU as the documented entry point for commercial products, and expect the compliance obligations that attach to federal systems and covered contracts. Where the sources are silent, particularly on measured adoption and returns, this analysis stays silent too.

https://www.svdg.org/.brief: The page presents Motiv, an agency run by Andrej Schindler and Jonas von der Gathen that describes itself as an "Agentur für Zukunftspotenziale", placing creative people with values-oriented companies. It says it connects people and companies, accompanies individual development and creates space for future perspectives, driven by curiosity about people and how organisations evolve. Companies are described as grown, unique organisms whose sense of purpose and urge to develop are their driving forces, and the agency says its aim is to place people who bring both professional expertise and the ability to connect with a company's purpose. It states that it works with companies holding social and ecological values and seeks long-term working relationships, and that it sees people as developing beings whose individual potential it tries to recognise at the right moment for a career step. The page also invites readers to register for a quarterly newsletter with open positions, accounts of company visits and interviews.

https://www.janes.com/.brief: Janes reports that it gathers information from vetted on-ground specialists, exclusive interviews, and events, acting as human sensors that web crawlers cannot reach. Janes reports that every data point is verified against reliable, vetted sources and that its dataset is the largest of its type, connecting millions of points to uncover patterns. Janes reports that its final content is peer reviewed to meet its quality and accuracy standards, and that it supplies validated data for the Joint Intelligence Preparation of the Operational Environment process. Janes reports that its digital portal lets users navigate validated data to uncover insights, moving from “what happened” to “what it means.”

https://www.govini.com/.brief: Govini says that Air is a leader in Enterprise Readiness and that its mission is to make readiness a real-time, continuously achieved condition. The company explains that its platform layer turns activated data into adaptive workflows, mobilized agents, and AI-driven orchestration that forecasts issues, prioritizes recommendations, and aligns resources.

https://theworldofai.org/ai-ecosystem/ec.brief: The page catalogues two organisations it classifies as government labs, each verified individually against a document the organisation published about itself, with the deciding source and the date it was last read recorded. It states that Technology Innovation Institute in Abu Dhabi operates under Abu Dhabi's Advanced Technology Research Council and has published frontier open models, while Shanghai AI Laboratory is described as a state-established Chinese research institution backed by national ministries and the Shanghai municipal government. The page argues that state-funded labs hold a distinct place in the AI ecosystem because they answer to public mandates and sovereign budgets rather than venture capital or product revenue. It adds that both institutions can in principle command infrastructure commitments, such as compute and facilities, that market-driven labs must negotiate for commercially. The page also says its classifications are not assigned by keyword, model, or inheritance from a parent company, on the grounds that a classification keeping no evidence cannot be audited.
